summary: A call to seek God while he is near and to turn back to him, for his plans and paths rise above ours as heaven above earth.

context.title: A call to return
paragraphs: Isaiah 55 speaks to Jews exiled in Babylon, whom the prophet urges not to settle for what cannot satisfy. [c1] It opens by inviting the thirsty to come and buy without money. [c2] Verse 3 promises an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies once shown to David. [c3]

The reading begins as the invitation turns into a summons to seek the LORD while he can be found. [c4] Verse 7 calls the wicked to leave their way and promises mercy to those who come back. [c5] Verses 10-11 follow with rain and snow that do not go back to the sky before watering the earth, an image of God’s word. [c6]

In synagogue practice Isaiah 55:6 to 56:8 is the prophetic lesson at the afternoon service of fast-days, though Sephardic Jews read no afternoon lesson from the prophets on fast-days except the Ninth of Ab. [c7] On those days the Torah reading recounts the Lord’s thirteen qualities of mercy from Exodus 34, the passage that today’s psalm echoes. [c8]

translationNotes.summary: Hebrew maḥashavah covers plans and purposes, not only passing thoughts: here it names what God intends to do.
translationNotes.body: The noun means thought, but also device, plan and purpose. [c9] Verse 7 uses it for the schemes of the wicked man, and verse 8 sets God’s own plans against human ones. [c10] Skinner’s Cambridge commentary takes God’s thoughts here as purposes of redemption, too vast for despairing minds. [c11] Jeremiah 29:11 uses the same noun for God’s plans of peace for the exiles. [c12]

translationNotes.summary: Derekh is a road or journey, and by extension a way of life: God’s roads run as high above ours as the sky.
translationNotes.body: Derekh is first a road or journey, then a course of life or action. [c13] Verse 7 asks the wicked man to abandon his own road, which the Pulpit Commentary glosses as his mode of life. [c14] Verse 9 measures the gap by the height of the heavens above the earth. [c15] Psalm 145:17, sung today, uses the same noun for the ways in which the LORD is righteous. [c16]

translationNotes.summary: Literally “he will multiply to forgive”: the verb salaḥ, forgive, is used in the Bible only of God.
translationNotes.body: The Hebrew reads literally “he will multiply to pardon,” as older commentators note. [c17] The verb salaḥ, to forgive or pardon, is used in the Bible only with God as its subject. [c18] The Pulpit Commentary contrasts this with people, who find it hard to pardon those who wrong them. [c19] Jewish teaching on repentance cites this verse for God’s loving-kindness towards the sinner who returns. [c20]

translationNotes.summary: Shuv, “return”, is a main biblical verb for repentance, and the chapter plays on it again with rain and with God’s word.
translationNotes.body: Shuv means to turn back or return, and with God as the goal it means to seek him penitently. [c21] Jewish tradition calls repentance teshubah, literally return, and names shub as one of its two biblical verbs. [c22] The same verb comes back in verses 10 and 11: rain and snow do not return to the sky without watering the earth, and God’s word does not return to him empty. [c23]

claims.text: Isaiah 55 is addressed to exiles in Babylon, who were in danger of losing their nationality and religion through devotion to material aims.
Isaiah 55:1 invites the thirsty to come and buy without money.
Isaiah 55:3 promises an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David.
Isaiah 55:6 calls the hearers to seek the LORD while he may be found; Skinner (Cambridge Bible) reads verses 6-7 as a call to repentance because of the nearness of the kingdom of God.
Isaiah 55:7 calls the wicked to forsake his way and return to the LORD, who will have mercy on him.
Isaiah 55:10-11 compares God’s word to rain and snow that do not return without watering the earth; the word is potent to effect its purpose.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Isaiah 55:6-56:8 is read as the haftarah at the afternoon service of fast-days, but the Sephardim read the afternoon haftarah only on the Ninth of Ab.
The fast-day Torah lesson (Exodus 32:11-14 and 34:1-10) treats the thirteen qualities of mercy, and Psalm 145:8 is taken almost verbatim from Exodus 34:6.
The Hebrew noun מַחֲשָׁבָה means thought, and also device, plan or purpose.
Isaiah 55:7 uses the same noun for the thoughts (plans) of the wicked man, which BDB lists under the sense device, plan, purpose; Isaiah 55:8 contrasts God’s thoughts with human thoughts.
Skinner (Cambridge Bible) holds that the thoughts and ways of God in Isaiah 55:8-9 are his purposes of redemption, too vast for the narrow conceptions of despairing minds.
Jeremiah 29:11 uses the same noun for God’s thoughts of peace towards the exiles.
The Hebrew noun דֶּרֶךְ means way, road, journey or manner, and figuratively a course of life or action.
Isaiah 55:7 asks the wicked to forsake his way, which the Pulpit Commentary explains as his mode of life.
Isaiah 55:9 compares the height of God’s ways above human ways to the height of the heavens above the earth.
Psalm 145:17 uses the same noun for the ways of the LORD, in all of which he is righteous.
The Hebrew of Isaiah 55:7 rendered “abundantly pardon” is literally “multiply to pardon”.
The Hebrew verb סָלַח, forgive or pardon, is always used of God.
The Pulpit Commentary contrasts God’s abundant pardon with people, who find it hard to pardon those who have offended them.
The Jewish Encyclopedia’s article on repentance quotes Isaiah 55:7 for God’s loving-kindness extended to the returning sinner.
The Hebrew verb שׁוּב means turn back or return, and with God as goal it means to turn back to him penitently.
In Jewish doctrine repentance is called teshubah, literally “return”, and biblical Hebrew expresses repentance with the verbs shub and niḥam.
The verb שׁוּב recurs in Isaiah 55:10-11: the rain and snow do not return without watering the earth, and God’s word does not return to him empty.
